# Two-Sided Difference Testing {#sec-two-sided-difference}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Learning objectives"}
- State the null and alternative for a two-sided difference test.
- Interpret the limitations of a non-significant result.
:::

## The idea

A two-sided difference test commonly uses the null hypothesis $H_0: \Delta=0$ against $H_1:\Delta\ne0$, where $\Delta$ is a consistently signed group difference. Planning specifies an anticipated alternative difference, alpha, power and appropriate variance model. This was previously described as an “equality” objective in the calculator; the teaching term **two-sided difference testing** is less misleading.

## When and how to apply it

The null hypothesis refers to the equality of population parameters under the model, not the study goal of proving that therapies are the same. Failure to reject $H_0$ does not imply equivalence or non-inferiority.

## Teaching case 1 — baseline draft

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" title="Clinical scenario / initial worked example"}
A trial expects a five-point difference in a symptom score; its null is zero difference and it plans 80% power under the specified alternative.
:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" title="Common error"}
“No statistically significant difference” is not evidence that the groups are clinically equivalent.
:::
